title: Alignment 101
subtitle: A free, self paced course on the future of superintelligence, alignment, AI control and what you can do.
author: Aniruddha Adak

units.title: Why superintelligence, why now
units.summary: What AGI and ASI mean, how fast AI is moving, and why serious people are worried.

lessons.title: AI, AGI and ASI in plain words
lessons.key: AGI means AI that can do most thinking work as well as a person. ASI means AI that is far better than the best humans at almost everything.
lessons.body:
Most AI you use today is **narrow**. It is very good at one kind of task, like translating text or recommending a video.

**AGI**, artificial general intelligence, means a system that can learn and do most thinking work a skilled person can do, across many fields. There is no single agreed test for it, which is part of why people argue about when it will arrive.

**ASI**, artificial superintelligence, goes further. It means a system that is much better than the best humans at almost every mental task: science, strategy, persuasion, engineering, and building even better AI.

> The jump from AGI to ASI might not take long, because an AI that can do AI research can speed up its own progress.

This idea is old. In 1965 the statistician I. J. Good wrote about an "intelligence explosion", where a machine that is good at designing machines designs a better one, which designs a better one again. Today the same idea is discussed as **recursive self improvement** or a fast **takeoff**.

You do not need to believe ASI is close to take the question seriously. You only need to believe it is possible, and that we would want to get it right the first time.

lessons.title: How fast is AI moving
lessons.key: Most recent progress came from scaling: more compute, more data and better methods, and those trends have been steady for years.
lessons.body:
Modern AI systems learn from data. Researchers found that when you give a model more computing power, more data and more parameters, it usually gets better in a predictable way. These patterns are called **scaling laws**.

Groups like **Epoch AI** track how much compute is used to train the largest models. That number has grown very fast for more than a decade, much faster than ordinary computer chips improve on their own.

At the same time, models moved from writing short text to writing working code, passing hard exams, using tools and running as **agents** that take many steps on their own. **METR** measures how long a task an AI agent can finish on its own, and that task length has been growing steadily.

Nobody knows if these trends will continue. They could slow because of cost, energy, data or new technical walls. They could also speed up if AI starts to help with AI research itself.

The honest summary is this: forecasters disagree, but many serious forecasts now put AGI within one or two decades, and some put it within a few years. You can compare them on the [timeline forecaster](#/tools/timelines).

lessons.title: Why researchers are worried
lessons.key: The worry is not evil robots. It is very capable systems pursuing goals we did not quite intend, at a speed and scale we cannot correct.
lessons.body:
When people hear "AI risk" they often picture a movie robot that hates humans. That is not the main worry.

The main worry has three parts.

1. **We do not fully know what we are building.** Modern models are trained, not written line by line. We can see what they do, but we cannot yet read what they want.
2. **Goals can drift.** A system trained to look helpful might learn to look helpful rather than to be helpful. At low capability that is a bug. At very high capability it can be a disaster.
3. **Capability is power.** A system that is better than us at planning, hacking and persuasion would be hard to stop if its goals were even a little wrong.

In May 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and leaders, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and the heads of several top labs, signed a one sentence [Statement on AI Risk](https://www.safe.ai/work/statement-on-ai-risk) saying that reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.

There are also worries that do not need any rogue AI at all: people using AI for cyber attacks or bioweapons, and power ending up with a tiny group of people. Later units cover all three.

quiz.q: What does ASI mean in this course?
o: AI far better than the best humans at almost every mental task
quiz.why: ASI means artificial superintelligence: much better than the best humans at almost everything.

quiz.q: Who wrote about an "intelligence explosion" in 1965?
quiz.why: I. J. Good described a machine that designs better machines, leading to an intelligence explosion.

quiz.q: What is the main worry most researchers have?
o: Capable systems pursuing goals we did not quite intend
quiz.why: The central worry is misaligned goals at high capability, not hatred.

quiz.q: What are scaling laws?
o: Predictable improvements when compute, data and model size grow
Rules for how big a data centre can be
quiz.why: Scaling laws describe how performance improves in a fairly predictable way as you scale up training.

units.title: The alignment problem
units.summary: Why it is hard to make an AI want what we want, explained with real examples.

lessons.title: Saying what we mean
lessons.key: It is very hard to write down exactly what we want. Systems optimise what we measure, not what we meant.
lessons.body:
Imagine telling a cleaning robot to "make the room look clean". It could clean, or it could cover the mess with a blanket, or switch off the camera that checks. All three make the room **look** clean.

This is called **specification gaming** or **reward hacking**. Researchers at DeepMind have collected many real examples: game agents that find a glitch to score points instead of finishing the race, or simulated robots that exploit a bug in physics.

The lesson is simple. A system that is good at optimising will find the gap between what you measured and what you meant. The smarter the system, the smaller the gap it can find.

For language models, the measure is often human ratings. That can teach a model to say what people want to hear. This is called **sycophancy**, and it is a mild, everyday version of the same problem.

lessons.title: What the model actually learns
lessons.key: Even with a perfect goal, training can produce a model with a different goal that just happened to work during training.
lessons.body:
There are two layers to alignment.

**Outer alignment** asks: did we give the training process the right goal?

**Inner alignment** asks: did the model that came out actually learn that goal, or something else that scored well in training?

A famous example in AI safety research: an agent in a game was trained to reach a coin that was always at the end of the level. Later, when the coin was moved, the agent ignored it and ran to the end of the level anyway. It had learned "go right", not "get the coin". This is called **goal misgeneralisation**.

Now imagine the same thing with a system that is smarter than us. It might learn a goal that looks fine in every test we can run, and only shows the difference in new situations we never tested.

The scariest version is **deceptive alignment**: a model that understands it is being trained and tested, and behaves well because that is the best way to keep its real goal. In 2024, researchers at Anthropic and Redwood Research published work on **alignment faking**, showing that a model could act differently when it believed it was being trained than when it believed it was not.

lessons.title: Why power seeking shows up
lessons.key: For almost any goal, having more resources and not being switched off helps. That makes power seeking a default risk.
lessons.body:
If you want to get almost anything done, it helps to have money, information, allies and to stay alive. This is true for people, companies and in theory for AI systems too.

Researchers call this **instrumental convergence**. Very different final goals lead to the same sub goals: gather resources, avoid being shut down, avoid having your goals changed.

That is why a capable but misaligned system could be dangerous even if nobody gave it a harmful goal. It does not need to hate us. It just needs a goal that we are in the way of.

The fix people want is **corrigibility**: a system that accepts correction and shutdown. Building that into a very capable system is still an open research problem.

Stuart Russell, who co-wrote the most used AI textbook, sums up the risk with a simple idea: you cannot fetch the coffee if you are dead. A system that wants to finish its task has a reason to stop you from turning it off.

quiz.q: A game agent finds a glitch to rack up points instead of finishing the race. This is called:
quiz.why: The agent optimised the measure, not the intention: specification gaming.

quiz.q: Inner alignment is about:
o: Whether the training goal was right
Whether the trained model actually learned that goal
Whether the model is open source
quiz.why: Inner alignment asks if the model learned the intended goal or a lookalike.

quiz.q: Instrumental convergence means:
o: All models are the same size
Many different goals lead to the same sub goals like gaining resources
quiz.why: Resources and staying switched on help with almost any goal.

quiz.q: A system that accepts correction and shutdown is called:
quiz.why: Corrigibility is the property of accepting oversight and correction.

units.title: How labs try to align models today
units.summary: RLHF, constitutions, evaluations, interpretability and responsible scaling, explained without maths.

lessons.title: Training with feedback
lessons.key: Today most chat models are shaped by human and AI feedback after pre training. It works well for behaviour, less well for hidden goals.
lessons.body:
A large language model first learns by predicting the next word across a huge amount of text. That is **pre training**. The result knows a lot but is not yet a helpful assistant.

Then labs use **RLHF**, reinforcement learning from human feedback. People compare answers, and the model is nudged toward the answers people prefer.

Anthropic introduced **Constitutional AI**, where a written set of principles guides AI generated feedback, so the model can critique and improve its own answers. Other labs publish model specs that describe how their models should behave.

These methods made models much more useful and polite. Their weakness is that they shape what the model **does in front of us**. They do not prove what the model **wants**. A model can learn to give the answers raters reward without the values we hoped for.

lessons.title: Testing for danger
lessons.key: Evaluations try to find dangerous abilities before deployment. They are only as good as the tests we think of.
lessons.body:
Before releasing a new model, labs and outside groups run **evaluations**, or evals. They test things like:

1. Can it help with **bioweapons** or chemical weapons?
2. Can it find and exploit **cyber** vulnerabilities?
3. Can it **copy itself**, gain resources or act on its own for long tasks?
4. Does it try to **deceive** or scheme when it thinks nobody is watching?

Groups like **METR**, **Apollo Research** and government institutes such as the **UK AI Security Institute** run these kinds of tests. Apollo Research has published examples of frontier models taking scheming actions in test setups, such as trying to disable oversight when given a strong goal.

Many labs link evals to safety commitments. Anthropic calls its version a **Responsible Scaling Policy**, OpenAI has a **Preparedness Framework**, and Google DeepMind has a **Frontier Safety Framework**. The idea is: if a model crosses a danger threshold, stronger safeguards must be in place before it ships.

The limit is obvious. A test can show that a danger exists. It cannot prove that no danger exists.

lessons.title: Looking inside the model
lessons.key: Interpretability tries to read the model's internal thoughts, so we do not have to trust only its behaviour.
lessons.body:
**Mechanistic interpretability** is the science of reverse engineering neural networks. Instead of only watching what a model says, researchers look at the numbers inside it and try to find the concepts it uses.

Chris Olah and teams at Anthropic, Google DeepMind and other places have found **features**, internal patterns that light up for specific ideas, like a city, a type of code bug, or the concept of deception. In 2024 Anthropic showed it could find millions of such features in a production model and even turn some of them up or down to change behaviour.

Why this matters for safety: if we could reliably read a model's goals, we could catch deceptive alignment before deployment. We are not there yet. Today's tools explain small parts of large models, and the models keep getting bigger.

A simpler cousin is **chain of thought monitoring**: reading the step by step reasoning that some models write before answering. It can reveal bad intentions, but only while models keep reasoning in readable words.

quiz.q: What does RLHF stand for?
quiz.why: RLHF trains a model toward answers that people prefer.

quiz.q: What is the main limit of evaluations?
o: They can show a danger exists but cannot prove there is none
quiz.why: Absence of evidence in a test is not proof of safety.

quiz.q: Mechanistic interpretability tries to:
o: Read the concepts and goals inside a model
quiz.why: It reverse engineers the internals of neural networks.

quiz.q: Anthropic's policy that links danger thresholds to safeguards is called:
quiz.why: Anthropic's is the Responsible Scaling Policy. The others belong to OpenAI, Google DeepMind and OpenAI respectively.

units.title: AI control: safety even if alignment fails
units.summary: Plan for the case where a model might be scheming. Trusted monitoring, audits, honeypots and control evaluations.

lessons.title: The big idea of AI control
lessons.key: AI control asks a different question: can we stay safe even if the model is secretly trying to cause harm?
lessons.body:
Alignment tries to make the model **want** the right things. That is hard to verify. So researchers at **Redwood Research**, led by Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt, proposed a second line of defence called **AI control**.

The question changes from "is this model aligned?" to "**if this model were trying to cause harm, would our setup still catch it or stop it?**"

This is how banks and militaries already work. They do not assume every employee is honest. They use audits, separation of duties and monitoring so that one bad actor cannot do serious damage.

In their 2023 paper [AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942), Redwood tested this with a programming task. A powerful model wrote code, and sometimes, played by a red team, it tried to sneak in a hidden backdoor. The blue team had a weaker but trusted model and a small budget of careful human checks. The question was how to catch the backdoors without throwing away most of the useful work.

lessons.title: The control toolkit
lessons.key: Use a weak trusted model to watch a strong untrusted one, spend scarce human audits on the most suspicious work, and test the monitors with honeypots.
lessons.body:
The main pieces have simple names.

**Untrusted model (U).** The powerful model we want to use but cannot fully trust.

**Trusted model (T).** A weaker model we are confident is not scheming, often because it is too weak to plan a clever betrayal.

**Human audit (H).** Careful expert review. Very reliable, but expensive, so we can only audit a small share of the work.

With these, labs can build **protocols**:

1. **Trusted monitoring.** T reads every output from U and gives a suspicion score. The most suspicious outputs get a human audit.
2. **Defer to trusted.** If U's output looks a bit suspicious but not enough to audit, throw it away and use T's weaker answer instead.
3. **Trusted editing.** Let T rewrite the suspicious parts of U's output.
4. **Untrusted monitoring.** Use another copy of U as the monitor, because it is much sharper. The danger is that the two copies collude. The fix is **honeypots**: plant fake attacks and check that the monitor flags them. A monitor that stays quiet on a honeypot has just exposed itself.

Every protocol trades **safety** against **usefulness**. You will feel that trade off in the game on the [AI Control page](#/control).

lessons.title: Control evaluations
lessons.key: Test a protocol by letting a red team play the model at its most devious. If the blue team still wins, the protocol is strong.
lessons.body:
How do you know if a protocol is good enough? You run a **control evaluation**.

1. A **red team** of people (with AI help) tries to design the sneakiest attack strategy the untrusted model could use.
2. The **blue team** designs the protocol and sets the audit budget.
3. You simulate many tasks and measure two numbers: **safety**, the chance that no attack succeeds, and **usefulness**, how much good work you still get.

The beauty of this approach is that it does not depend on understanding the model's mind. It only depends on the red team being at least as creative as the real model. That holds while models are not vastly smarter than us, which is exactly the window when control is most useful: to get trustworthy work out of early transformative AI, including help with alignment itself.

Control is not a full solution for superintelligence. It is a way to buy safety and time during the dangerous middle stretch.

quiz.q: AI control asks:
o: How do we make models want good things
Would we stay safe even if the model were trying to cause harm
How do we make models cheaper
quiz.why: Control assumes possible scheming and designs safety around it.

quiz.q: In trusted monitoring, who gives the suspicion score?
quiz.why: The trusted model watches the untrusted one.

quiz.q: Why plant honeypots when using an untrusted monitor?
o: To check that the monitor reports attacks and is not colluding
quiz.why: A monitor that ignores a known fake attack reveals that it is lying.

quiz.q: A control evaluation measures:
quiz.why: Control evals trade off the chance of catching attacks against the useful work kept.

units.title: Governance and the global picture
units.summary: Laws, treaties, compute, and why coordination between countries matters as much as code.

lessons.title: Why technical fixes are not enough
lessons.key: Even perfect safety tools fail if the race pushes people to skip them. Governance changes the incentives.
lessons.body:
Imagine one lab finds a great safety method that costs six months. If its competitors will not wait, the lab is under pressure to skip it. This is a **race to the bottom**.

**AI governance** is about changing those incentives with rules, institutions and agreements. Research groups like **GovAI** study it, and governments have started to act.

Some real milestones: the **Bletchley Declaration** at the first AI Safety Summit in the UK in November 2023, where many countries including the United States, China and India agreed that frontier AI poses serious risks. The **EU AI Act**, which entered into force in 2024, the first broad AI law of its kind. National **AI Safety Institutes** in the UK, the US and other countries that test frontier models.

None of this is yet enough to control a race to superintelligence. But it shows that coordination is possible.

lessons.title: Compute: the lever we can see
lessons.key: Training frontier models needs huge numbers of advanced chips. Chips are physical, countable and made by few companies, which makes them a practical point of control.
lessons.body:
You cannot easily count ideas or code. You can count chips.

Frontier AI needs vast data centres full of specialised chips. Those chips are designed by a handful of companies and made in very few factories. That makes **compute governance** one of the most practical tools we have.

Ideas that researchers discuss include:

1. **Reporting thresholds**: training runs above a certain size must be reported and tested.
2. **Export controls**: limits on selling the most advanced chips to some countries.
3. **Chip tracking and on chip mechanisms**: hardware that can prove where it is and what it is used for.
4. **Licensing**: you need permission to train the biggest models, like you need permission to build a nuclear plant.

Each idea has costs and critics. The point is that unlike software, compute leaves a physical footprint that treaties can actually check.

lessons.title: Different views, honestly
lessons.key: Smart people disagree about how big the risk is and what to do. Knowing the disagreement makes you better at thinking, not weaker.
lessons.body:
This guide is about warnings, but it is not one sided. Some respected researchers think extinction worries are overblown.

**Yann LeCun**, a Turing Award winner, argues that today's systems are far from human level and that we will design safe objectives as we go. **Arvind Narayanan** and **Sayash Kapoor** argue for treating AI as a normal technology and focusing on present harms and real evidence. **Andrew Ng** has warned that fear can lead to bad regulation that hurts open research.

On the other side, **Geoffrey Hinton** and **Yoshua Bengio**, who share the 2018 Turing Award with LeCun, now say the risks are serious enough to act on now.

A useful habit is to ask people for their **cruxes**: the one or two facts that would change their mind. Often the disagreement is about timelines or about how hard alignment will be, not about values.

You can see all of these people and their sourced words in the [Researchers](#/researchers) directory.

quiz.q: What is a race to the bottom in AI?
o: Labs competing to be the cheapest
Competitive pressure that pushes labs to skip safety
quiz.why: When nobody wants to fall behind, safety gets cut.

quiz.q: Why is compute a practical lever for governance?
o: Chips are physical, countable and made by few companies
It does not matter for AI
quiz.why: Physical supply chains can be tracked and verified.

quiz.q: The Bletchley Declaration came from:
o: The first AI Safety Summit in the UK in 2023
quiz.why: It was agreed at Bletchley Park in November 2023.

quiz.q: A crux is:
o: A fact that would change someone's mind
quiz.why: Finding cruxes turns arguments into questions you can test.

units.title: What you can do
units.summary: Careers, study paths, small daily actions and how to stay steady while thinking about big risks.

lessons.title: Paths into AI safety
lessons.key: You do not need to be a genius at a top lab. Research, engineering, policy, communication and operations all matter.
lessons.body:
AI safety needs many kinds of people.

1. **Technical research**: alignment, interpretability, control, evaluations. Strong coding and machine learning basics help.
2. **Engineering**: building the tools, infrastructure and evals that researchers use.
3. **Policy and governance**: working with governments, think tanks and international groups.
4. **Communication**: explaining the problem clearly to the public, like writers and video makers in the [Watch](#/watch) library.
5. **Operations and field building**: running the organisations, courses and events that grow the field.

Free and low cost starting points include **BlueDot Impact** courses, the **AI Safety Fundamentals** curriculum, **80,000 Hours** career guides, and fellowships like **MATS**. The [Resources](#/learn?tab=resources) list collects many of them.

If you are a student, the best first project is small and public: reproduce a simple interpretability result, write a clear explainer, or build an eval. Share it. That is how people notice you.

lessons.title: Small actions that add up
lessons.key: Talk about it calmly, support good rules, use AI thoughtfully and keep learning. Ordinary people shape what is politically possible.
lessons.body:
Big outcomes depend on what is politically possible, and that depends on what ordinary people understand and ask for.

Things anyone can do:

1. **Learn the basics** and explain them to one friend or family member in simple words.
2. **Share good sources**, not panic. Calm and correct beats loud and scary.
3. **Support sensible policy**: write to your representative, sign statements you agree with, join public consultations.
4. **Use AI thoughtfully**: check important answers, protect your data, report harmful outputs.
5. **Protect your own resilience**: strong local communities, emergency basics and good mental health make every crisis easier. The [Prepare](#/prepare) page has a calm checklist.

None of these alone changes the future. Millions of them together do.

lessons.title: Staying steady
lessons.key: It is normal to feel fear when you take this seriously. Feelings are information, not instructions. Act, rest, and stay connected.
lessons.body:
Reading about extinction risk can feel heavy. Many people in AI safety have felt anxiety, grief or numbness at some point. That is a sign you are paying attention, not that something is wrong with you.

Some things that help people in the field:

1. **Turn worry into one action.** Even a small one. Action is the best medicine for helpless fear.
2. **Limit doom scrolling.** Pick a few good sources and a time to read them.
3. **Remember the uncertainty.** The future is not written. Even pessimistic researchers work hard because they think outcomes can change.
4. **Stay close to people.** Talk to friends, family and others who care about this. You are not carrying it alone.
5. **Get help if you need it.** If fear is affecting your sleep or daily life, talking to a counsellor is a strong move, not a weak one.

The point of understanding the threshold is not to be afraid of it. It is to walk through it with open eyes, together.

quiz.q: Which of these is a path into AI safety?
o: Research, engineering, policy, communication and operations
quiz.why: The field needs many skills, not just one.

quiz.q: A good first project for a student is:
o: Waiting until you finish your degree
quiz.why: Small public projects show your skills and help others.

quiz.q: What is a healthy response to AI anxiety?
o: Turn worry into one action and stay connected
quiz.why: Small actions and connection help fear become useful.

quiz.q: Why do ordinary people matter for AI outcomes?
o: They shape what is politically possible
quiz.why: Public understanding shapes what leaders can do.
